messages.subject: Ex-Gaussian distribution
parts:
Hello,
 I'd like to ask if you could implement Ex-Gaussian distribution in STAN. The distribution is described in http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponentially_modified_Gaussian_distribution . Since my mathematical skills are non-existent, I would be greatful for help :)

Best regards,
 Marcel

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Ex-Gaussian distribution
parts:
On Friday, January 4, 2013 11:45:24 AM UTC-5, Marcel Falkiewicz wrote:
 I'd like to ask if you could implement Ex-Gaussian distribution in STAN. The distribution is described in http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponentially_modified_Gaussian_distribution . Since my mathematical skills are non-existent, I would be greatful for help :)

Thanks for the suggestion. I imagine it will be implemented in Stan eventually, which would make it possible to optimize the calculation of the derivatives a bit. In the meantime, it is easy enough to use this (log) density in Stan with something like:

data {
  int<lower=1> N;
  real y[N];
}
transformed data {
  real sum_y;
  sum_y <- sum(y);
}
parameters {
  real mu;
  real<lower=0> sigma;
  real<lower=0> lambda;
}
model {
  real half_lambda;
  real sigma2;
  real sqrt_2;
  real summands[N];

  half_lambda <- 0.5 * lambda;
  sigma2 <- square(sigma);
  sqrt_2 <- sqrt(2.0);

  // log-likelihood
  lp <- lp + log(half_lambda) + half_lambda * (2 * mu + lambda * sigma2);
  lp <- lp - lambda * sum_y;
  for(n in 1:N) {
    summands[i] <- log(erfc( (mu + lambda * sigma2 - x[n]) / (sqrt_2 * sigma) ));
  }
  lp <- lp + sum(summands);
  // optional priors on parameters
}

messages.subject: Re: Ex-Gaussian distribution
parts:
Bah, all my instances of lp should have two trailing underscores, as in lp__ . And you could calculate the square root of 2 in the transformed data block rather than the model block.

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Ex-Gaussian distribution
parts:
On Sunday, January 6, 2013 5:26:29 PM UTC-5, Marcel Falkiewicz wrote:
 thanks to your help, I think I've managed to understand the most general way of implementing PDs in STAN :-). However, I'm curious if there's a way to use these C++-free models in other model files, just like the distributions that are supplied with STAN?

If I understand you question correctly, you are asking whether it is possible to write a function once using the Stan language, save it somehow, and subsequently use that function? In which case, the answer is no, not yet. For the time being, you would need to copy and paste the implementation repeatedly (which is why we would encourage everyone to post to this list any customized log densities they have needed to write). 

On the other hand, writing a C++ implementation is not particularly hard even if you don't know much C++. If you know some coding language, you can probably make a copy of the file that implements the exponential

https://code.google.com/p/stan/source/browse/src/stan/prob/distributions/univariate/continuous/exponential.hpp 

and then modify it to implement the Ex-Gaussian. After that, there is a bit more work in terms of writing tests to make sure it works correctly and getting the parser to recognize that a new density is available, but we would certainly help you with that if you wanted to undertake it.

Ben

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Ex-Gaussian distribution
parts:
On Sunday, January 6, 2013 7:47:33 PM UTC-5, Marcel Falkiewicz wrote:
Another question then: is it possible to concurrently use two functions in Stan language (each computing it's own log-likelihood) in the same model? For example, if I had an ex-Gaussian implementation (as you provided) and let's say a translated Weibull distribution and wanted to estimate a model with common parameter for both of these functions y ~ exnorm(mu,sigma,tau) and z ~ tweibull(mu, sigma,theta). Do I just add log-likelihoods for these custom distributions? Or is it more tricky than that?

It isn't more tricky than that in Stan. The reason is that Stan essentially is just making an accept / reject decision for a proposed joint parameter vector for a log-posterior distribution (with a somewhat involved mechanism for generating proposals). So, if a parameter contributes to the log-posterior in multiple ways that is fine mathematically. Unlike BUGS, Stan doesn't have to figure out the full-conditional distribution of mu, which would be complicated in your example.

Ben

parts:
Hello,
 I was pleased to notice that exponentially modified Gaussian distribution was actually implemented in Stan, for which I would like to thank you very much. However, there seems to be a problem with fitting the lambda parameter. Parameter estimates of lambda converge to a very small value. However, mu and sigma seem to converge to correct values. Attached you will find stan code for simple ex-gaussian fitting, a file containing real RT data and R code to reproduce this effect, comparing parameter estimates to those produced by retimes R package. Note that I've tested the same model on simulated data, the results are always the same - lambda/tau parameter gets very small, while mu and sigma remain correct.

Regards,
 Marcel

parts:
Hi Marcel,

The retimes package doesn't describe how it's "ex-Gaussian" is parameterized. Stan's parameterization is in the manual.

I think 1 / tau will match the retimes package. Here's an updated Stan program:

data {
  int<lower=1> N;
  real RT[N];
}
parameters {
  real<lower=0> mu;

real<lower=0> sigma;
  real<lower=0> lambda;
}

transformed parameters {
  real<lower = 0> tau;
  tau <- inv(lambda);
}
model {
  // Priors
  mu ~ normal(2000, 1000);

  //
  RT ~ exp_mod_normal(mu, sigma, lambda);
}


I don't know what you're trying to do with the gamma priors. I just dropped them.


Daniel

  half_lambda <- 0.5 * lambda;
  sigma2 <- square(sigma);
  sqrt_2 <- sqrt(2.0);

  // log-likelihood
  lp <- lp + log(half_lambda) + half_lambda * (2 * mu + lambda * sigma2);
  lp <- lp - lambda * sum_y;
  for(n in 1:N) {
    summands[i] <- log(erfc( (mu + lambda * sigma2 - x[n]) / (sqrt_2 * sigma) ));
  }
  lp <- lp + sum(summands);
  // optional priors on parameters
}

>>> It isn't more tricky than that in Stan. The reason is that Stan
>>> essentially is just making an accept / reject decision for a proposed joint

>>> mechanism for generating proposals). So, if a parameter contributes to the
>>> log-posterior in multiple ways that is fine mathematically. Unlike BUGS,
